name: map-string
axis: string-keyed hash map: insert, hit/miss lookup, iterate
n: n=100000 distinct keys, r=150 lookup passes over a 2n probe array (30M lookups: 15M hit, 15M miss), 1 values() iteration
nPython: n=25000, r=150 (4x fewer keys and 4x fewer lookups; everything scales linearly in n)
notes: Probe keys are built in their OWN loop so a probe string is a different object from the equal-content key that was inserted. That matters a lot: with the SAME object reused, VL's `__str_eq__` short-circuits on `ref.eq` and a 10M-hit loop measures 497ms instead of 1042ms — a 2.1x difference. All four runtimes have that shortcut, so reusing the objects would have made the benchmark measure nothing. VL cannot express the natural miss test: `const v = m[k]; if v != null` is `vl check`-clean but an EMIT ERROR ('bare null needs a struct-typed context') for an i32-valued map, so all four use the `?? -1` sentinel instead. Structural notes: Rust uses the default SipHash-1-3 hasher (a real handicap, but swapping it is a third-party library change); Python and V8 cache a string's hash in the string object, VL recomputes it over an `array i32` of code points every probe. Key CONSTRUCTION is a measured VL weakness that partly loads this benchmark: building 600k `"key"+toString(i)` strings costs VL 449ms vs JS 83ms, Rust 49ms, Python 106ms; here the build phase is ~15-20% of VL's total.
